facts.claim: KDA's chunk kernels are slow because of an inter-chunk serial dependency
facts.value: REFUTED. Three independent measurements: (1) time scales LINEARLY with B*h (work-scaled 0.98 from B=8) -- a chain's latency does not grow with batch; (2) halving chunk_size to 32 DOUBLES the chain length and is 19% FASTER (T=4096: 12.12 -> 9.81 ms), the reverse of the chain prediction; (3) the genuinely sequential kernels (fwd_kernel_h grid 512, bwd_kernel_dhu grid 256) are 1.51 of 12.77 ms = 11.9% of KDA time. The real cause is OCCUPANCY: the four dominant kernels achieve 6-12% occupancy and run at 15-29% of HBM and 16-42% of SM, while every kernel above 80% occupancy runs at 85-93% of HBM peak. Grid size is ample (8192-131072 blocks on 78 SMs); the kernels burn too many registers/shared memory per block, leaving ~4-8 resident warps with nothing to hide memory latency. Latency-bound, not chain-bound, not bandwidth-bound, not grid-bound. Measured DRAM traffic: 14.79 GB in 12.77 ms = 1.16 TB/s, 29% of the 4 TB/s peak.
facts.uncertainty: one layer in isolation, uncompiled and without fp8; the in-model kernels could differ. The T-sweep criterion (ns/token flat from T=1024) is weak on its own -- proofs 1 and 2 are what discriminate.
facts.boundary: the occupancy lives inside fla's Triton/TileLang kernels. Fixing it means editing or rewriting fla, and rewriting is already refuted (tileRL measured its own TileLang GDN 9.3x slower than fla on H20).
facts.refuted_by: an ncu run showing high occupancy in the dominant KDA kernels

Applied to the in-model fla group (~102 of the 128.1 ms DeltaRecurrence total; short_conv is unaffected) that is ~19.5 ms/step, 2.0% of the 978.5 ms step.
facts.uncertainty: the intra-chunk work is O(chunk^2) so halving it halves that term, which is why more serial steps still wins. NOT tested: chunk_size changes the chunking of the same math, so numerics shift slightly.

facts.value: The training loss path slices head.weight[:Cfg.vocab] into Liger FLCE, which has no per-class mask: the alignment-padding rows (vocab_real:vocab) entered the softmax denominator at their random-init values. Inference (lm_logits) masks at vocab_real; the training path never did. Fixed 2026-08-30 by zero-initializing the padding rows after self.apply(self._init) (commit 06d52cd): padding logits stay 0, and the rows are never targets so CE gradient only pushes them down. The padding's measured contribution is the constant offset log(32784/32773) = 0.00034 (step-0 delta in every run). The 32776 A/B passed not because the defect was absent but because 3 random columns rarely spike; the defect existed there too, and the zero-init fix is what makes both configs clean.
facts.source: runs/ab_vocab.log (32773 vs 32776), runs/ab_vocab_32784.log, runs/ab_vocab_32784_zeroinit.log, runs/ab_vocab_32784_lr003.log (pod); train.py FLCE slice head.weight[:Cfg.vocab]; fix commit 06d52cd

facts.uncertainty: The +-1.7 swings at LR_SCALE=0.1 were first misattributed to the padding rows; the zero-init run swung identically, proving the swings are chaotic-regime compounding of the width difference itself (the baseline arm 32773 trains smoothly on the old sample in the 32776 A/B but chaotically on the rebuilt sample at LR 0.1). The padding rows' own contribution is the 0.0003 constant offset, isolated at step 0. Single run per cell.
facts.boundary: The A/B's three criteria (max |delta| at noise floor, no growth, no systematic sign) are only meaningful in a STABLE training regime; in a chaotic regime they fail for any width change. The 32776 pass was regime-luck as much as column-count luck. This is the criteria's ceiling, not an execution failure -- same family as b0's 8.4pt (formula right, wrong source) and corpus_fp_matches reporting 1/7 yet PASS: a check that passes for reasons unrelated to what it checks. Run the vocab A/B at AB_LR_SCALE=0.03 (the stable regime on the current sample; 0.1 swings +-1.7).

facts.claim: how the 27B scoring service is started, so the next person does not have to rediscover it
facts.value: Two INDEPENDENT single-card servers, one process each: http://127.0.0.1:8100 (GPU4) and http://127.0.0.1:8101 (GPU5), OpenAI-compatible, 28.4 GB each. NOTE FOR CALLERS: the model emits a <think> block first (Qwen3.8 thinking mode), so a scorer must either disable thinking in the prompt or parse past it before reading the answer. READINESS: probe with a real 1-token completion, never /v1/models -- the first deployment answered /v1/models while its engine was dead.
facts.source: started by the tileRL session; command recorded below verbatim

config.weights: /data00/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 (NVFP4 only -- the bf16 copy is broken, MMLU 0.0%)
config.command: per card, two separate processes: setsid nohup bash -c 'cd /work/tilerl && export PYTHONPATH=/work/tilerl/src:/work/tilerl/packages/tilerl-kernels/src TILELANG_CACHE_DIR=/work/tilelang_cache TILERL_TARGET=cuda TILERL_QWEN38_SOURCE=/data00/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=<4|5> && python -m tilerl.cli serve --model qwen38-27b --host 0.0.0.0 --port <8100|8101>' &
config.devices: ONE CARD PER PROCESS, and --devices is deliberately NOT passed. cli.py:56-81: --devices builds a DataParallelEngine, which is replicas inside ONE process; a CUDA error in one replica is sticky for the whole process, so one card's failure takes the other down while HTTP keeps answering. Omitting --devices takes the plain build_engine path, pinned by CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES.
config.cuda_graph: ON. Engine.__init__ sets _decode_graph_on = decode_graph and draft is None; serve takes no --draft, so the graph stays on. Passing a draft would silently disable it and cost 7.9x at B=1 (11.6 -> 91.6 ms/tick).

facts.uncertainty: First deployment used --devices 0,1 and died before serving any scoring traffic: /v1/chat/completions returned cudaErrorStreamCaptureInvalidated and engine.py:717 _make_kv threw AcceleratorError in a loop, while /v1/models still answered. GPU4 had dropped 26.7 -> 11.2 GB, GPU5 held 26.8 -- one replica dead, one alive, same PID. VERIFIED: --devices means one process (code plus the single PID across both cards). INFERRED, NOT PROVEN: that concurrent CUDA-graph capture between the two replicas is what invalidated the capture. The single-card split removes the shared-process failure mode either way. No throughput or concurrency measurement; sized for 400 documents.
facts.boundary: the service is this session's; scoring prompts, acceptance criteria and their facts belong to the scoring session
facts.refuted_by: the recorded command failing to bring the service up on a clean pod

facts.claim: the 27B scoring service's KV pool can back the token budget it declares
facts.value: REFUTED. cli.py:66 sets num_blocks=256 and max_total_tokens=8192, but kv_cache.py:37 has BLOCK_TOKENS=16, so the pool holds 256 x 16 = 4096 tokens -- HALF the declared budget. A scoring request of prompt ~2000 + thinking output up to 661 is ~2661 tokens = 167 blocks, so TWO concurrent requests need 334 > 256 and the pool is exhausted: 'RuntimeError: PagedKvPool exhausted: all 256 blocks in use' at kv_cache.py:124 alloc_block, after which the engine loop throws on every request. Safe concurrency at that context length is 1, not 4. This is the true cause of the scoring caller's 0/3 run, which was first attributed to the caller's 16-way concurrency.
facts.source: kv_cache.py / cli.py read against the scoring session's error report

config.service: tilerl serve --model qwen38-27b, one process per card
config.request_shape: prompt ~2000 tok + thinking output up to 661 tok = ~2661 tok = 167 blocks
config.observed_failure: 16-way concurrency from the caller; 2-way is already over the pool

facts.uncertainty: the block arithmetic is exact; the ~2661-token request shape is the caller's report, not measured here
facts.boundary: the service was delivered after a SINGLE-request smoke test with no capacity limit stated, so the caller had no way to know. Raising num_blocks is the fix and is cheap -- the 27B in NVFP4 uses about 28 of 96 GB -- but the right value must be computed from the KV tensor size, not guessed. Not done: the line was paused before restart.
facts.refuted_by: a run at 2-way concurrency with ~2661-token requests that does not exhaust the pool

facts.claim: the fp8 quantize overhead is a second, transposed cast per tensor, and no torchao config removes it at a profit
facts.value: torchao 0.17.0 casts input, weight and grad_output TWICE per step -- once per GEMM, in two different layouts. The second is the transposed one, and it is 59% of the fp8 overhead (71.08 of 120.12 ms at batch 32; the four largest kernels in the group all carry _t_ in their inductor names). Float8LinearConfig exposes six cast configs for exactly this, and ROWWISE_WITH_GW_HP is the one recipe that removes two of them: it sets cast_config_input_for_grad_weight and cast_config_grad_output_for_grad_weight to ScalingType.DISABLED, so grad_weight runs in bf16 and its transposed fp8 casts never happen. REJECTED on arithmetic: the three GEMMs have identical FLOPs (all MKN), so moving grad_weight from fp8 to bf16 costs about a third of the 247.25 ms fp8 GEMM row at half throughput, roughly +82 ms, while the entire fp8 quantize row is only 60.93 ms. Even removing ALL of the quantize overhead loses. Separately it scales AXISWISE, which is what makes stock `rowwise` raise 'aten.clone.default with axiswise scaling is not supported yet' under compile on the AttnRes .chunk() path, so it is very likely unrunnable here as well.
facts.source: torchao/float8/config.py:353-379 and float8_linear.py:95-150 read directly; kernel split from probes/profile_step.py on GPU 0

config.recipe_in_use: e4m3_tensorwise (train.py:402, a custom config, not a stock recipe)
config.note: the 60.93 ms / 247.25 ms figures are the batch-16 table; the 120.12 ms / 71.08 ms split is this batch-32 profile

facts.uncertainty: the one-third split of the fp8 GEMM row across the three GEMMs is from equal FLOP counts, not a per-GEMM measurement. The conclusion does not depend on it: the entire quantize row is smaller than the cost of moving one GEMM to bf16.
facts.boundary: torchao 0.17.0. A future version that fuses the transposed cast into the GEMM epilogue, or a grad_weight kernel that reads a non-transposed operand, reopens this.
facts.refuted_by: a measured ROWWISE_WITH_GW_HP run that is net faster end to end

facts.claim: how much val NLL a throughput saving is allowed to cost before it stops paying for itself
facts.unit: nat of val NLL per e-fold of training tokens (local slope, 0.2b-0.3b segment)
facts.source: ladder points p02 (0.2b, 3.691), p03 (0.3b, 3.322), p04 (0.4b, 3.159); each entry is a secant slope over its own segment

config.use: A saving of x fraction of step time buys 1/(1-x) times the tokens in the same wall clock, so it is worth up to slope*ln(1/(1-x)) nat of quality. Worked: Block AttnRes saves 10.7% of step -> 1.120x tokens -> tolerance 0.103 nat. Below that the time it buys back more than covers the quality it costs.
config.why_this_matters: Names the tolerance BEFORE the sample size, so n cannot be chosen for affordability and the tolerance backfilled to match.
config.measured_drift: The rate is not a constant and the drift is fast: one point later the slope had fallen 38% and the tolerance with it, 0.103 -> 0.064. A tolerance quoted without the segment it came from is wrong within one budget point. Always recompute at the budget being decided.
config.which_changes_this_binds: Only changes that COST quality. A throughput change that costs none (short_conv, an fp8 recipe) is a pure wall-clock win and keeps its full value as D grows -- there the conversion is 1% of step ~ 20 min per 34h ladder. The two currencies move in OPPOSITE directions as D grows: absolute time saved rises, quality-equivalent value falls. Do not use one rate for both.

facts.uncertainty: Every entry is a secant, so each overestimates the local slope at the right edge of its own segment. Two secants imply a curvature that would put the 3.24b slope far below 0.567 -- but that is the chained extrapolation this fact exists to discourage, so it is a reason to expect the fitted answer to be severe, not a number to cite. The six-point fit supplies the local slope; until then quote the segment, never a single rate.
facts.boundary: the 0.2b-0.3b segment of this mix and architecture; recompute the local slope at the budget being decided
facts.refuted_by: the six-point ladder fit giving a local slope at 3.24b that this two-point estimate misses by more than its own uncertainty

facts.value: --fp8 casts the whole model to bf16 before training (train.py:1626) and run_ddp.sh always passes --fp8, so there are no fp32 master weights: the optimizers hold bf16 parameters, their state is bf16, and every step() rounds the result back to bf16. Fraction of parameter ELEMENTS whose bf16 bit pattern is unchanged across optimizer.step(), by lr_scale: 1.0 -> 32.00%, 0.5 -> 48.38%, 0.2 -> 71.56%, 0.1 -> 84.19%, 0.05 -> 91.29%, 0.01 -> 98.26%. The schedule's own floor is final_lr_frac=0.05 with warmdown=0.65, so a run spends its last 65% of steps decaying into the regime where 91.3% of updates are discarded. bfloat16 carries 8 mantissa bits, so an update below ~2^-9 of a parameter's magnitude cannot change its bit pattern: it is computed, applied, and dropped with nothing raising. A stalled parameter is indistinguishable from a converged one on the loss curve, which is why this needed a bit-level count rather than a loss reading.
facts.unit: percent of parameter elements unchanged per optimizer step
facts.source: E2E_GPU=6 python probes/bf16_update_loss.py --ckpt ckpt_p324.pt --steps 6 --batch 4; runs/bf16_update_loss.log and runs/bf16_update_loss2.log

config.ckpt: ckpt_p324.pt (all 176 tensors bfloat16; no optimizer state saved)
config.data: data/sft/sft_all.pt, real tokens and real gradients
config.path: train.py's own build_optimizers + convert_to_fp8_compute, torch.compile off
config.comparison: bit-level on the int16 view, not allclose: two equal bf16 values ARE the same value

facts.uncertainty: Measured on a pretrained checkpoint with SFT data; gradient magnitudes at the midpoint of a fresh 30B pretrain may differ. The 32% floor at full LR includes parameters whose gradient is legitimately zero (never-used vocabulary rows among them), so the absolute level is an upper bound on discarded WORK; the 32% -> 91% movement with LR is the signal and is unambiguous.
facts.boundary: Counts discarded updates, not the quality they would have bought. The loss cost needs an A/B against fp32 master weights. READING RULE, or this number is misread as its own refutation: fp32 master weights do NOT lower this figure. The model stays bf16, so a single small update is still rounded away on write-back; what changes is that the optimizer's fp32 copy RETAINS it and it accumulates until it crosses the bf16 threshold. So the A/B must report two lines -- frozen[model bf16], high in both arms and not a failure, and frozen[optimizer], equal to the first in the control and ~0% with masters. Mechanism confirmed on CPU (tilerl): same seed, same data, lr=1e-5, 400 steps, bf16 elements whose bit pattern actually moved was 1/144 without masters and 126/144 with them.
